case_name: London Drugs Ltd. v. Red Deer (City)
text:
Alberta Court of Queen's Bench

London Drugs Ltd. v. Red Deer (City)

Date: 1987-09-10

T.W. Wakeling, for
plaintiffs.

N.P.W. Riebeek, for defendant.

(Red Deer No. 8510-02601)

September 10, 1987.

[
1
]

M
ason

J.:–

Introduction

[
2
]

The plaintiffs by statement of claim seek a
declaration that the Hours of Business By-law of the city of Red Deer, By-law
No. 2870/85, is ultra vires, illegal, invalid, void and of no force or effect
and/or that it is inconsistent with
s. 2(
a
) and (
c
) and
s. 15
of
the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
and is of no force or effect.

[
3
]

The by-law is designed to restrict the
commercial activities of retail sales businesses in the city, with certain
exceptions, to specific hours each day with closure on Sunday unless the
business establishment closes to the public for a period of 24 consecutive
hours in one of the six days immediately following Sunday.

[
4
]

The plaintiffs are both major retail sales
businesses in the city of Red Deer. They have been operating a seven-day work
week. The plaintiffs attack the by-law on the basis that the by-law would
require them to close one day each week and because of the focus of the by-law,
that day might well be Sunday.

[
5
]

The several grounds upon which the plaintiffs
seek a declaration of invalidity from the court, while recited in the statement
of claim, were presented in argument in the form of four questions to be
answered on the basis of an agreed statement of facts. Two of the questions
raise the issues of the constitutionality of the by-law under
ss. 2
and
15
of the

Charter
, one question raises the vires of portions of the by-law under the
provisions of the
Municipal Government Act of Alberta, R.S.A. 1980, c. M-26
, as
amended, and one question attacks the wording of the by-law for uncertainty.

[
6
]

The agreed statement of facts identifies the
plaintiff London Drugs Limited as an extra-provincial corporation in Alberta
carrying on a major drug store and food merchandising retail business in the
city of Red Deer and elsewhere. The plaintiff The Brick Warehouse Ltd. is described
as an Alberta corporation carrying on a major retail furniture business in Red
Deer and elsewhere. The defendant, city of Red Deer, is described as a
corporation pursuant to the provisions of the
Municipal Government Act, R.S.A.
1980, c. M-26
.

[
7
]

The agreed statement of facts recites that the
impugned by-law was passed by the city of Red Deer on 12th November 1985 and
attaches a copy of the by-law as Schedule A. There then follows a recitation of
a number of demographic statistics relating to the population of the defendant
city, the various religious preferences of its people, the estimated labour
force, and categorization and estimates of the number of persons employed in
retail and service trade outlets, essential services and recreational facilities,
as well as hospital and government offices. Most of this information is taken
from a booklet entitled “Red Deer Central Alberta: The Future is Now”, which is
attached as Sched. B to the agreed statement of facts.

[
8
]

The agreed statement of facts and the attached
by-law are included as Appendix I to these reasons.

[
9
]

The substantive portions of the by-law required
to be considered by the court on the basis of the questions put forth are as
follows:

2. In this By-law,

(
a
) “Area of Business Establishment”
means the area of the business establishment as calculated for business tax
purposes and as recorded in the records of the City Assessor. Where no such
record is kept, area shall mean the total area of the business establishment as
the same would be calculated for business tax purposes.

(
b
) “Business” means the selling of
goods or services for consumption or use and not for resale and includes the
selling of goods or services by hawkers, pedlars and transient traders.

(
c
) “Business Establishment”,
“establishment”, “premises”, “shop”, or “store”, in the appropriate case, means
the premises, building, booth, stall or place where a business is carried on
and includes any booth, stall or place where goods are exposed or offered for
sale or by public auction.

(
d
) “Person” includes a natural
person, a partnership, a corporation and any of their officers, agents or
employees.

(
d.
1) “Convenience Store” means a
business establishment which sells only miscellaneous food and grocery items,
dairy products, books, magazines, newspapers, cigarettes, candy, snack food and
a selection of miscellaneous items.

(
e
) “Sell” or “selling”, “sale”,
“sold”, “sales”, in the appropriate case includes offering for sale or
attempting to sell or barter directly or indirectly on any pretense or by any
device whatsoever.

3. No person shall conduct business in the
City of Red Deer between the hours of 12:00 p.m. and 6:00 a.m. on any day of
the week.

4. On a Sunday, no person shall conduct
business or admit members of the public to a business establishment in the City
of Red Deer unless during any period of 24 consecutive hours in the 6 days
immediately following the Sunday the premises are closed to the public and no
goods or services are sold to the public.

6. Sections 3 and 4 do not apply to a
convenience store where the total area of the business establishment is less
than 3000 square feet.

7. Section 4 does not apply to a business
establishment containing a pharmacy within the meaning of the Pharmaceutical
Association Act where the total area of the business establishment is less than
3000 square feet.

8. Section 4 does not apply where the only
goods offered or available for sale are:

(
a
) potted plants and accessory
supplies, flowers and floral arrangements, horticultural supplies, bedding
plants, nursery stock, and in conjunction therewith, accessory gardening and
lawn care supplies but not including garden and lawn equipment;

(
b
) those goods that are available
for sale at a greenhouse, Market Garden or householders garage sale; or

(
c
) handicrafts.

11. Section 4 does not apply to a grocery
store, groceteria or food store of an area of 18000 square feet or less.

12. Sections 3 and 4 do not apply to a taxi
business, hotel, motel or restaurant.

14. Any person who contravenes Section 5 of
this By-law is guilty of an offence and shall be liable upon conviction to a
penalty not exceeding $1,000.00 plus costs, and in default of payment to
imprisonment for up to 60 days.

15. Any person who contravenes Section 3 or
4 of this By-law is liable on summary conviction on a first offence to a
minimum fine of $1,000.00 and a maximum fine of $2,000.00; on a second offence
to a minimum fine of $2,000.00 and a maximum fine of $5,000.00; on a third
offence to a minimum fine of $5,000.00 and a maximum fine of $10,000.00. In addition
to a fine the Court may, in each case direct payment of costs and direct that
in default of payment of the fine, the person be imprisoned for a period not
exceeding 6 months.

16. Every person who authorizes or directs
anything to be done in contravention of Section 3 or 4 is liable on summary
conviction on a first offence to a minimum fine of $1,000.00 and a maximum fine
of $2,000.00; on a second offence to a minimum fine of $2,000.00 and a maximum
fine of $5,000.00; on a third offence to a minimum fine of $5,000.00 and a
maximum fine of $10,000.00. In addition to payment of a fine, the Court may in
each case direct payment of costs and may direct that in default of payment of
the fine, the person being [sic] imprisoned for a period not exceeding 6 months.

[
10
]

The omitted ss. 5, 9, 10 and 13 deal
respectively with closing on Remembrance Day and exemptions from the one-day
closing provision for fuel, motor oils, auto and machinery parts sales,
cinematic productions and the operation of educational, recreational and
cultural facilities, and public facilities operated by schools and communities.

[
11
]

The four questions submitted for answer although
not in the order stated by the parties are:

I. i) Whether By-law No. 2870/85 of The
City of Red Deer is outside the jurisdiction of The City of Red Deer in that
the
Municipal Government Act,
R.S.A. 1980, c. M-26, s. 241(2),
authorizes by-law makers to exempt businesses based on “size
or
type”
[emphasis added] and not on size or type or both, the classification system adopted
by By-law No. 2870/85.

ii) And, whether The City of Red Deer
further exceeded its jurisdiction in enacting penalties in sections 15 and 16
of By-law No. 2870/85 not authorized under section 110 or 244 of the
Municipal
Government Act.

II. Whether By-law No. 2870/85 of The City
of Red Deer in utilizing phrases such as those set out in
sections 2
(d.1), 6,
8(b), 11 and 12 is void because it introduces sufficient uncertainty so as to
make it impossible to apply the By-law sensibly.

III. Whether By-law No. 2870/85 of The City
of Red Deer is of no force and effect because its purpose is to influence
retailers to close on Sunday in compliance with the view of some Christians
that Sunday is the Lord’s Day and it violates the concept of separation of
church and state enshrined in
section 2(1)
of the
Canadian Charter of Rights
and Freedoms
(“Charter”) and enunciated in
The Queen v. Big M Drug Mart
Ltd.,
[19851
1985 CanLII 69 (SCC)
, 1 S.C.R. 295.

IV. Whether By-law No. 2870/85 of The City
of Red Deer is of no force and effect because it discriminates against large
retailers and does not reasonably promote the objective of ensuring that at
least one day in the week remains substantially free of commercial activities,
thereby contravening
section 15
of the
Charter
.

[
12
]

In
L.S.U.C v. Skapinker,
1984 CanLII 3 (SCC)
, [1984] 1 S.C.R.
357, 11 C.C.C. (3d) 481, 9 D.L.R. (4th) 161 at 181, 8 C.R.R. 193, 3 O.A.C. 321,
53 N.R. 169, the Supreme Court of Canada said:

The development of the
Charter
as it takes
its place in our constitutional law, must necessarily be a careful process.
Where issues do not compel commentary on these new Charter provisions, none
should be undertaken.

Accordingly, I have arranged the four questions
in the above order so as to consider the non-Charter issues first.

I

[
13
]

Has the city passed legislation beyond its
legislative competence?

[
14
]

By-law 2870/85 as an hours of business and shop
closing by-law by which the city of Red Deer regulates the days and hours
during which businesses must close is authorized by
s. 241
of the
Municipal
Government Act, R.S.A. 1980, c. M-26
, which says:

241(1) In this section, “businesses” means
businesses, shops or industries.

(2) A council may by by-law regulate and
control the days or hours or both that businesses are required to close, and
without limitation may

(
a
) exempt a business or 1 or more
classes of businesses, designated as to size or type, as to the number of
employees or as to the type of goods or services sold or offered for sale, from
any provision of the bylaw;

(
b
) impose conditions that must be
met by a business or 1 or more classes of businesses that are permitted to
remain open;

(
c
) provide that designated
businesses may remain open or closed according to a system of rotation.

(3) A council may by by-law authorize the
carrying on of business in emergencies or in other prescribed circumstances
during the days or hours when a business, or class of businesses, is required
to be closed under a by-law made under this section.

(4) A by-law under this section does not
apply to

(
a
) a fair or exhibition that is
lawfully held,

(
b
) a bazaar for charitable or
religious purposes, or

(
c
) a business the days or hours of
which are regulated pursuant to an Act of the Legislature.

[
15
]

This is the section of the Municipal Government
Act which provides the legislative foundation for passing an hours of business
by-law: see
R. v. Debaji Foods Ltd.
(1981),
1981 ABCA 109 (CanLII)
, 124 D.L.R. (3d) 254, 30 A.R.
143 (C.A.), at p. 146.

[
16
]

The city of Red Deer has exempted businesses
from the regulation and control of its “Hours of Business By-law” on the basis
of size
and
type, in ss. 6, 7 and 11 of the by-law.

[
17
]

Has the city council of Red Deer violated the
“immemorial” rule that the power to make by-laws does not permit the enacting
of regulatory provisions which discriminate unless such a power is expressly
conferred by enabling legislation? See
Montreal v. Arcade Amusements Inc;
Montreal
v. Fountainhead Fun Centres Ltd.,
1985 CanLII 97 (SCC)
, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 368, 29
M.P.L.R. 220, 18 D.L.R. (4th) 161 at 188 and 189, 58 N.R. 339 [Que.], in
particular the cite of Louis-Philippe Pigeon, in Redaction et Interprétation
des Lois (1978), at p. 34, and also
Calgary v. S.S. Kresge Co.; Calgary v.
Super S. Drugs Ltd.
(1965),
1965 CanLII 508 (AB SCTD)
, 51 W.W.R. 747 (Alta. T.D.), at p. 754, Milvain
J. (as he then was).

[
18
]

The plaintiffs argue that the city may
discriminate only on the basis of size or type, not both size and type.
Legislating size and type, they argue, is ultra vires the enabling legislation.

[
19
]

The plaintiffs’ argument is based on the
proposition that the word “or” must be read disjunctively for the following
reasons: first, the grammatical presumption that “and” is conjunctive and “or”
is disjunctive except where the context, in which either word appears, requires
that the opposite meaning be given to the word used; second, the use of the
word “or” in the initiating clause of s. 241(2) that a council may “regulate
and control the days or hours or both” is a clear indication by the draftsman
that in this particular section “or” is used disjunctively; third, that
whenever “or” is used in para. (
a
) of s. 241(2) the use of “and” would
be inappropriate. The plaintiffs stated their arguments on this point in this
manner:

By virtue of
section 241(2)
(a) council can
decide to exempt just one business or more than one business. “[A] business or
1 or more classes of business” clearly conveys this meaning. Third, section
241(2)(a) obliges council, if it decides to exempt businesses, to select one
distinguishing feature of those businesses it wishes to exempt. It must select
one of the following characteristics: (1) size (2) type (3) number of employees
(4) type of goods sold (5) type of services available. This is not an
unreasonable interpretation.

[
20
]

I am unable to accept any of the plaintiffs’
points of argument. The interpretation of the bedevilling word “or” can only be
done having regard to the intention of the writer within the context or sense
of how the word is used: see
Clergue v. H.H. Vivian & Co.
(1909),
1909 CanLII 5 (SCC)
, 41
S.C.R. 607 at 617, Anglin J.:

There is no doubt of the intention of the
parties; and, where sense requires it, there are many cases to shew that we may
construe the word “or” into “and”, and “and” into “or”, in order to effectuate
the intent of the parties.

[
21
]

Section 241(2) plainly discloses the intent of
the legislature to give a council powers to exempt classes of business from the
operation of an hours of business by-law under broad cumulative discriminatory
bases. Nothing is said in the wording of s. 241(2)(
a
) nor is there
anything therein stated from which it can be inferred that these bases of
discrimination are not equally applicable in any one or more combinations.
These bases of discrimination are not presented as alternatives where only one
basis of discrimination may be utilized and not others. They are potentially
cumulative under ordinary grammatical construction.

[
22
]

By subs. (2), the power to exempt is “without
limitation”. Further, when one reads the subsection as a whole and considers
the use of “or” throughout, it carries the meaning that “X” or “Y” or “X and Y”
is the true import. A good example is “sold or offered for sale”. It would be
commercially illogical to interpret this phrase to mean that a shop be
classified on the basis of goods which it actually sold or goods which it
offered for sale.

[
23
]

Taken to its logical conclusion, the plaintiffs’
argument reduces itself to the proposition that the city may not do what it has
done in one by-law but it could do so by passing separate exempting by-laws
based on a single basis of discrimination.

[
24
]

The second part of the question is – has the
city enacted penalty provisions in s. 15 and s. 16 of the by-law which are not
authorized by the Municipal Government Act?

[
25
]

The following propositions are stated by Rogers,
The Law of Canadian Municipal Corporations, 2nd ed., vol. 1, p. 474.

1. [A]ny sanctions applied must be imposed
in accordance with the statutory or charter provisions in that behalf.

2. [A]ny penalty imposed for the infraction
of a by-law upon persons in a manner or to an extent not authorized is bad.

3. Where an Act stipulates how a by-law is
to be enforced, it cannot be enforced in any other manner.

[
26
]

Thus, there must be statutory authority for the
penal provisions of a by-law and the manner of their imposition.

[
27
]

The plaintiffs allege that the city has enacted
penalty sections which prescribe penalties that go beyond the authorizing
sections of the Act, namely, s. 110 and s. 244.

[
28
]

Section 110(1)(
a
) states as follows:

110(1) A council may by by-law

(
a
) impose a fine not exceeding
$2500, exclusive of costs, for contravention of any by-law under this or any
other Act and provide for reasonable punishment by imprisonment for any period
not exceeding 6 months in case of non-payment of the fine and costs imposed for
any such contravention, unless the fine and costs including the costs of
committal are sooner paid.

Section 110(2) and 110(3) state:

(2) A council may enact a general penalty
by-law for a contravention of any by-law or of any number of specified by-laws,
and may impose a fine and costs and imprisonment in the case of non-payment of
the fine and costs as set out in subsection (1)(
a
) and of the payment in
addition to the penalty as set out in subsection (1)(
b
).

(3) A council may, either in a general
penalty provision in a by-law or in a penalty provision applicable to a
contravention of a particular provision of a by-law, provide for

(
a
) a minimum fine, which shall be
imposed by a court on a conviction for a contravention of the by-law,

(
b
) minimum and maximum fines
applicable to 2nd or subsequent offences,

(
c
) a minimum daily fine not
exceeding $2500 for every day that the offence continues after conviction,

(
d
) any combination of fines
authorized by this subsection, or

(
e
) a minimum period of imprisonment
in case of non-payment of the fine and costs, which period may vary for first,
second and subsequent offences but shall not exceed 6 months in respect of one
offence.

Section 244 is stated in the following terms:

244 Notwithstanding section 110, a council
may by by-law impose, for the contravention of a by-law made under section 241
or 242,

(
a
) a fine of not more than $2000 for
a first offence;

(
b
) a fine of not less than $2000
and not more than $5000 for a 2nd offence;

(
c
) a fine of not less than $5000
and not more than $10 000 for a 3rd or subsequent offence.

[
29
]

The plaintiffs submit that penalty ss. 15 and 16
of the by-law are ultra vires on two grounds:

(a) first that the sanction of a minimum fine
for a first contravention of the by-law is not authorized by the enabling
penalty provisions of s. 244 of the Act; and

(b) second, having adopted and imposed fines for
contraventions of the by-law under the provisions of s. 244 of the Act, a
council cannot exceed the enabling provisions of s. 244 by also imposing
imprisonment in the event of failure to pay such fines and costs.

[
30
]

Both these grounds raise the same argument but
relate to different cross-over provisions adopted by the defendant, from both
s. 244 and s. 110 of the Act, in drafting the penalty sections by the bylaw.

[
31
]

The plaintiffs argue that the structure of the
Municipal Government Act “suggests” that a council must choose and adopt
penalty provisions which are authorized by one section or the other section of
the Act and must not use the sections in tandem.

[
32
]

The plaintiffs cite as authority for their
argument the decision in
R. v. The Brick Warehouse Ltd.,
Alta. Prov.
Ct., Action No. C0200096320A01, 1986 (not yet reported), at pp. 13 and 14,
where Aime Prov. J. states:

The Municipal Government Act under s. 244
states, “Notwithstanding section 110, a council may by by-law impose, for the
contravention of a by-law made under section 241 or 242 [closing by-laws], (
a
)
a fine of not more than $2000 for a first offence; (
b
) a fine of not
less than $2000 and more than $5000 for a 2nd offence; (
c
) a fine of not
less than $5000 and not more than $10 000 for a 3rd or subsequent offence”.

Section 110 of the Municipal Government Act
states, “(3) a council may, either in a general penalty provision in a by-law
or in a penalty provision applicable to a contravention of a particular
provision of a bylaw, provide for (
a
) a minimum fine, which shall be
imposed by a court on a conviction for a contravention of the by-law”.

The Webster’s International Dictionary
interprets the word “notwithstanding” as “without prevention or obstruction
from or … in spite of. Had the legislators intended that there be a minimum
penalty for the first offence they could have very easily said so as they
followed section 110 in the second and third offences of section 244. The city
therefore has exceeded their statutory authority.

[
33
]

Section 110 is the general penalty section for
the contravention of any by-law under the Municipal Government Act or any other
Act. Subsection (1) enables a council to impose a fine not exceeding $2,500
exclusive of costs or punishment by imprisonment not exceeding six months for
non-payment of the fine and costs, for contravention of any by-law under the
Municipal Government Act or any other Act.

[
34
]

Subsection (2) permits enactment of a general
penalty by-law by a council.

[
35
]

Subsection (3) allows a council by a general or
specific penalty provision in a by-law to provide for:

(a) a minimum fine on conviction for
contravention of the by-law;

(b) minimum and maximum fines applicable to
second or subsequent offences;

(c) a minimum daily fine up to $2,500 for
continued contravention after conviction;

(d) and combination of fines authorized by subs.
(3); and,

(e) a minimum period of imprisonment for
non-payment of fines and costs not to exceed six months in respect of any
offence.

[
36
]

Section 110(3)
(
a
)
grants explicit authority to a
council to impose a minimum fine on conviction for a contravention of a by-law.
There is no limit in application of subs. (3)(
a
) to first, second, third
or subsequent offences. Council may therefore set a minimum fine even for a
first offence under this provision.

[
37
]

Section 110(3)(
e
) enables a council to
impose imprisonment terms not exceeding six months for non-payment of fines and
costs. And subs. (3)(
d
) permits these to be done in combination.

[
38
]

I find, therefore, on this explicit wording that
there is definite statutory authority granted a council to import these
provisions into the penalty provisions of a by-law and in any combination.

[
39
]

Section 244 is a specific penalty section in the
Act. Authority to utilize its enabling provisions is restricted by the section
itself to bylaws passed under the authority of ss. 241 and 242 of the Act,
those being the hours of business by-laws and the hours of entertainment
by-law, respectively. Section 244 therefore has application to the bylaw in
question.

[
40
]

By virtue of its “notwithstanding section 110”
clause, this section at one and the same time overrides, but is supplemental
to, the general penalty authorizing section of s. 110. It does not purport to
take exclusive jurisdiction as the only enabling penalty section. In this
context, “notwithstanding” is used in its prepositional sense to mean “in spite
of or “regardless”.

[
41
]

Further the use of the word “may” in both ss.
110 and 244 supports this interpretation. According to
s. 25(2)
(
c
) of
the
Interpretation Act, R.S.A. 1980, c. I-7
, ” ‘may’ shall be construed as
permissive and empowering”. Thus s. 244 permits a municipal council to impose
larger fines for second and subsequent contraventions without being obstructed
by the $2,500 maximum set out in the general penalty section, s. 110. But, in
doing so, it is restricted to a slightly lesser maximum for first
contraventions.

[
42
]

In my opinion, s. 244 does not derogate from the
enabling provisions of s. 110 beyond the point that: in framing its general
penalty provisions in an “Hours of Business” by-law, if the city elects to act
under s. 244 for specifically permitted larger fines overall for second and
subsequent contraventions, it must draft within the limits set out and adopted
in s. 244. It cannot mix limits of fines under s. 244 with the limits set out in
s. 110. Having said that, however, I find that the additional authority to levy
costs and imprisonment, in effect the enforcement provisions, are not at all
ousted by the “notwithstanding” clause of s. 244. Both sections are compatible
and should be so read and applied. Contrary to the “structure” argument put
forward by the plaintiffs, I am of the opinion that the structure of the Act is
straightforward and should be interpreted in the manner I have stated.

[
43
]

With respect, I am unable to accept the reasoning
of Provincial Court Judge Aime in
R.
v. The Brick Warehouse Ltd.,
supra.

[
44
]

The simple answer to this question is that the
by-law in no way offends the provisions of the Act.

II

[
45
]

Is by-law 2870/85 void for uncertainty?

[
46
]

The plaintiffs cited the general rule that a
by-law should be certain and definite and argued that much of the Red Deer
by-law is uncertain. The defendant submitted that a by-law must be interpreted
in light of the legislating body’s intention, and that all interpretation
should be “fair, liberal and large”, and in accordance with
s. 10
of the

Interpretation Act, R.S.A. 1980, c. I-7
. On this basis, the defendant contended
the by-law is not void for uncertainty at all.

[
47
]

These seemingly different rules reflect only two
of the approaches to the multi-faceted difficulties faced by courts in
interpreting by-laws. The plaintiffs cited
Hirsch v. Winnipeg Beach
(1961),

1961 CanLII 392 (MB CA)
, 26 D.L.R. (2d) 659 (Man. C.A.), at p. 668 for the proposition that “The law is
clear that a by-law must be clear [sic] and definite”. However, this statement
is made by Miller J.A. in a separate concurring judgment. Schultz J.A. (Adamson
C.J.M. concurring) stated the rule at p. 664, that “municipal by-laws passed in
good faith and pursuant to statutory authority should be benevolently interpreted
and, if possible, made operative.”

[
48
]

The plaintiffs also relied on
Can. Occidental
Petroleum Ltd. v. North Vancouver
(1983),
1983 CanLII 539 (BC SC)
, 46 B.C.L.R. 179, 148 D.L.R. (3d)
255 (S.C.), at p. 264, quoting
Re Dartmouth and S.S. Kresge Co.
(1966),

1966 CanLII 501 (NS CA)
, 58 D.L.R. (2d) 229 at 234 (N.S.C.A.), that a by-law “must be certain and
positive in its terms”. However, Locke J. in that case also recognized the rule
that if one possible interpretation results in validity, while another results
in invalidity, the interpretation which achieves validity should be used.

[
49
]

Both sides cited Halsbury’s Laws of England, 4th
ed. (vol. 28, para. 1329) that a “byelaw must provide a clear statement of the
course of action which it requires to be followed or avoided”. The defendant
city emphasized the portion which says that all need not appear on the by-law’s
face. However, I think that the closing sentence is most helpful for my
purpose:

… if the words of the byelaw are ambiguous
but their meaning can be resolved to give a reasonable result the courts will
give effect to that result.

Thus, if there is a possible meaning, the by-law
should not be struck down for uncertainty.

[
50
]

The authority given for this proposition is Lord
Denning in
Fawcett Properties Ltd. v. Buckingham County Council,
[1961]
A.C. 636 at 677, [1960] 3 W.L.R. 831, [1960] 3 All E.R. 503 (H.L.)
:

… a by-law will be void for uncertainty if
it can be given no meaning or no sensible or ascertainable meaning. But if the
uncertainty stems only from the fact that the words of the by-law are ambiguous,
it is well settled that it must, if possible, be given such a meaning as to
make it reasonable and valid, rather than unreasonable and invalid.

Lord Cohen in the same case at p. 662 said that
a court should not strike down a by-law for uncertainty “unless it is
impossible to resolve the ambiguity which it is said to contain.”

[
51
]

Galligan J. applied the ratio of the
Fawcett
case
in
Harrison
v. Toronto
(1982),
1982 CanLII 1998 (ON HCJ)
, 39 O.R. (2d) 721, 31 C.R. (3d)
244, 19 M.P.L.R. 310, 140 D.L.R. (3d) 309 (H.C.), in which the phrase “enclosed
in-door area being used as a place of public assembly” was argued to be
uncertain. He concluded (p. 315 M.P.L.R.):

… I am quite unable to say that there is no
sensible or ascertainable meaning to [the by-law’s] words. And if it can be
said that some of the words of the section, either individually or in
combination, might lead to a possible ambiguity, it is my opinion that
any
such ambiguity can be resolved by applying the ordinary English meaning of
those words to the facts disclosed by the evidence in an individual case.
[emphasis
added]

[
52
]

Rogers, The Law of Canadian Municipal
Corporations, 2nd ed., vol. 1, discusses the principles of by-law
interpretation. According to the authors (at pp. 390 and 472), if a by-law
derogates from common law rights, a strict interpretation is appropriate
(Meredith and Wilkinson’s Canadian Municipal Manual (1917), p. 254). But if it
only regulates or controls the exercise of rights for proper purposes it should
be subject to the general principle of benevolent interpretation (p. 471).

[
53
]

In
R. v. Debaji Foods
[supra] the Alberta
Court of Appeal considered a similar hours and closing by-law with a list of
exempted businesses which was being attacked for uncertainty. The court held
that a benevolent interpretation was appropriate to such a by-law as Stevenson
J.A. stated on behalf of the court at pp: 146-47:

Counsel for the respondent stressed that
the court should give a benevolent interpretation to the by-law and that every
effort should be made to sustain it consistent with ordinary rules of
construction. Difficulty in interpretation is not to be confused with vagueness
and uncertainty to the point of invalidity … We accept these general
principles.

[
54
]

Therefore, unless common law or other rights are
being derogated from, a by-law should be benevolently interpreted and should
only be found to be void if it is truly uncertain, and not merely vague or
difficult to interpret.

[
55
]

Ambiguity or indefinite wording or vagueness
does not necessarily constitute uncertainty. To be uncertain the words must be
such that a reasonable effort at interpretation will be unable to determine its
purpose. The test to be applied is that found in
Montreal v. Arcade
Amusements Inc.
[supra] at p. 251 [M.P.L.R.]:

“… the vagueness must be so serious that the
judge concludes that a reasonably intelligent man, sufficiently well-informed
if the by-law is technical in nature, is unable to determine the meaning of the
by-law and govern his actions accordingly.” [translation]

[
56
]

Nor is difficulty in interpretation the same as
“uncertainty to the point of invalidity”:
Re North Vancouver Shops
Regulation By-law,
1972 CanLII 1000 (BC SC)
, [1972] 2 W.W.R. 625, 24 D.L.R. (3d) 305 (sub nom.
Re
London Drugs Ltd. and North Vancouver
(B.C.S.C.);
Re Bent,
1940 CanLII 438 (BC SC)
, [1940] 2
W.W.R. 697 (B.C.S.C.);
Neilson Engr. Ltd. v. Toronto,
1967 CanLII 250 (ON HCJ)
, [1968] 1 O.R. 271,
66 D.L.R. (2d) 218 (H.C.);
Re Rolling Lands Ltd. and Hamilton-Wentworth,
Regional Mun.
(1980),
1980 CanLII 1619 (ON HCJ)
, 31 O.R. (2d) 624, 119 D.L.R. (3d) 317 (Div. Ct.);
Montreal
v. Arcade Amusements Inc.,
supra.

[
57
]

However for a court to interpret a by-law so as
to make it operative, the intention of the enacting body must be clear. McGillivray
J.A. states this general rule along with an important caveat in
Springbank
v. Render,
1936 CanLII 202 (AB SCAD)
, [1936] 2 W.W.R. 430, [1936] 4 D.L.R. 193 (Alta. C.A.), at p.
436:

… when passed
bona fide
in the
interest of the community pursuant to statutory authority and that, as in the
case of statutes, they should not be reduced to a nullity by a draftsman’s unskillfulness
if this can at all be avoided … But in all the cases in which the Court has in
fact modified the literal language of an enactment which I have been able to
find, the intention of the enacting body was manifest although poorly
expressed.

[
58
]

His caveat is that one cannot conjecture as to
council’s intention.

[
59
]

Re Rolling Lands,
supra, and
Hadden v. R,
1983 CanLII 2013 (SK QB)
, [1983] 3 W.W.R. 661, 21 M.P.L.R. 243,
23 Sask. R. 303 (Q.B.), affirm that interpretation is to be based on council’s
intention, where that intention is apparent.
Harrison
v. Toronto
,
supra,
states that the court has a
duty
to enforce council’s policy if that
policy is apparent from clear and explicit words and this may be gleaned from
the preamble as well as the by-law as a whole.

[
60
]

By-laws may also be rendered certain not only by
rules of construction but by evidence, to resolve questions of fact (
Hadden
v.
R.,
supra,
Re Rolling Lands,
supra). As well, individuals may
conduct a modest investigation to determine whether they fall within the
parameters of the by-law (
McGowan
v. Maryland,
366 U.S. 420, 6 L.Ed.
2d 393, 81 S. Ct. 1101
(1961)). Unfortunately, the scope of a “modest
investigation” is not defined. Nor can it be. But such an investigation must
surely extend, in such a case as this, to fact finding within the scope of
common retail commercial knowledge and accepted retail business customs and
practices to establish common standards of definition and accepted norms. The
matter must be susceptible of truth by evidence as opposed to opinion, that is,
the inquiry must be with respect to questions of fact not opinion.

[
61
]

There is no doubt as to the intention of the
defendant in passing the by-law in question.

[
62
]

The stated objects of the by-law, set out in its
recitals, are:

(a) to restrict the hours of business within the
city of Red Deer in order that commercial activity might be confined within
reasonable limits;

(b) to ensure that at least one day in the week
remains substantially free of commercial activities so that the citizens of Red
Deer might benefit thereby and be permitted to engage in family, social,
recreational and other activities so as to enhance the quality of life and to
generally promote the health and welfare of the citizens.

[
63
]

The recitals also state that the object of the
by-law is secular in nature and that the city wishes to enact a by-law
consistent with the rights and freedoms guaranteed to every Canadian by the

Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
.

[
64
]

Based upon the clearly expressed intention and
purpose of the by-law I am persuaded that it should receive a benevolent
interpretation.

[
65
]

The specific sections of by-law 2870/85 attacked
by the plaintiffs and alleged to be uncertain so as to render the by-law
impossible to apply and thereby void are:

(a) Section 11 is too vague. There are no clear
definitions of “grocery store”, “grocer”, and “groceteria” such that it is
questionable whether they may or may not encompass a store which sells goods
other than “staple food stuffs”, “meats and other foods” and “household
supplies”. For example, would a retail business which sells groceries and
pharmaceutical goods be defined as a grocery or pharmacy? Further, the
plaintiffs complain that the boundaries referred to in the sections are by
themselves indefinable.

(b) Section 12: The term “restaurant”, without
further definition, is too uncertain.

(c) Section 6: The definition of “convenience
store” uses the term “miscellaneous”, which, through its generality, robs
“convenience store” of ascertainable meaning.

(d) Section
8
(
b
): The phrase
“goods that are available for sale at a
…
householders garage sale” is
uncertain.

[
66
]

The exemptions in the by-law, with which the
plaintiffs mainly take umbrage, are those which define exemptions based on the
category or type of business, i.e., convenience store, grocery store, groceteria,
restaurant. The plaintiffs attack only certain categories, while other
categories such as taxi business, hotel and motel are apparently accepted.

[
67
]

The categories of “grocery store” and “groceteria”
are challenged as being uncertain in the absence of any definition. The alleged
uncertainty is based on the overlapping of various dictionary definitions.
“Restaurant” as a category is also not defined. The plaintiffs attack the
“convenience store” category on an alleged uncertainty introduced by its
definition in s. 2(
d.
1) of the by-law.

[
68
]

With respect, I am unable to find the use of
common general retail categories to describe businesses which are exempted from
the provisions of the by-law as too vague or indefinite to be uncertain.

[
69
]

Generally speaking, these categories or types of
businesses can be easily ascertained and the by-law applied without difficulty.
And the problem of defining the combined types of businesses, as illustrated by
the plaintiff London Drugs Limited, or new or fringe types of business
operations, to determine if the by-law applies or not to such categories can be
resolved by a simple and straightforward investigation into the commercial
world of retail sales to establish the facts.

[
70
]

Therefore, I must reject the proposition of the
plaintiffs that these common types or categories of business are too vague and
thereby uncertain. With particular reference to grocery store and groceteria, I
need only refer to
Re Rolling Lands Ltd.,
supra, and
Groceteria Ltd.
v. T. Eaton Co.,
1925 CanLII 288 (AB SCAD)
, 22 Alta. L.R. 92, [1926] 1 W.W.R. 1, [1926] 1 D.L.R. 26
(C.A.), to support my determination that they are capable of definition within
the intent and purpose of the by-law.

[
71
]

The plaintiffs’ argument that s. 12 of the
by-law must also be invalid for uncertainty because it utilizes the category of
“restaurant”, I am, with respect, unable to accept. They rely on the use of
Re
Hamilton Hospitality Indust. Assn. Inc. and Hamilton
(1981),
1981 CanLII 1957 (ON HCJ)
, 32 O.R. (2d)
353, 122 D.L.R. (3d) 266 (Div. Ct.), which has been distinguished, I believe
properly, by such later decisions as
Harrison,
supra, as well as
Re Kakamousias
and Pizza Pizza Ltd.
(1984),
1984 CanLII 2124 (ON HCJ)
, 46 O.R. (2d) 508 (Co. Ct.). In any event, I
decline to follow the
Hamilton Hospitality
case on the basis of my
previously stated reasons on common general retail categories and my assessment
that the learned judge applied too stringently the ratio of
R. v. Sandler,
1971 CanLII 478 (ON HCJ)
, [1971]
3 O.R. 614, 21 D.L.R. (3d) 286 (C.A.).

[
72
]

However, by defining a “convenience store” as
one which “sells only miscellaneous food and grocery items, dairy products,
books, magazines, newspapers, cigarettes, candy, snack food
and a selection
of miscellaneous items
” (my emphasis), the defendant has, in my opinion,
created a sufficient degree of vagueness to nullify the definition. Further, by
providing this definition of a “convenience store” in the by-law, the defendant
has negatived any factual investigation to define a “convenience store” within
the accepted norms of current retail business operation.

[
73
]

In its submissions, the defendant conceded that
in theory no specific items could be excluded under the phrase “a selection of
miscellaneous items”. However, they argued that through the application of the ejusdem
generis rule, the phrase referred to a small assortment of items which must be
sold in conjunction with other listed items. Such a proposition is of no help.
The definition is imprecisely worded, and awkwardly phrased. “[A] selection of
miscellaneous items” permits many postulations of what goods may be sold within
such a classification of goods. Obviously different people would have different
opinions as to what may or may not be sold. The phrase smacks too closely of
the uncertainty of similar phrases dealt with by the courts in such cases as
Swan
City Foods Ltd. v. R.
(1983),
1983 CanLII 1076 (AB QB)
, 27 Alta. L.R. (2d) 261, 23 M.P.L.R. 1, 48
A.R. 249 (sub nom.
Swan City Foods Ltd. v. Grande Prairie
) (Q.B.),
Dartmouth
v. S.S. Kresge Co.
[supra] and
Re Bunce and Cobourg,
1963 CanLII 181 (ON CA)
, [1963] 2 O.R.
343, 39 D.L.R. (2d) 513 (C.A.).

[
74
]

It follows therefore that s. 6 is also too
uncertain to be capable of proper interpretation, the definition of “convenience
store” being pivotal to its application.

[
75
]

That being the case, it is necessary to
determine whether these parts of the by-law may be severed without a rewriting
of the by-law. Before dealing with this issue, I should examine the remainder
of the by-law to determine if there are any other portions which may be invalid
due to uncertainty.

[
76
]

The plaintiffs raise an objection with respect
to s. 8 and in particular s. 8(
b
). Section 8 exempts from the
requirement of a one day closing each week those businesses “
…
where the only
goods offered
…
for sale are”:

(
a
) potted plants and accessory
supplies, flowers and floral arrangements, horticultural supplies, bedding
plants, nursery stock, and in conjunction therewith, accessory gardening and
lawn care supplies but not including garden and lawn equipment;

(
b
) those goods that are available
for sale at a greenhouse, Market Garden or
householders garage sale;
or

(
c
) handicrafts. (emphasis added)

[
77
]

As stated previously, the object of the by-law
is to regulate retail sales businesses and as such is directed at retailers who
are open for business throughout the week. Section 8 provides exemptions from
the application of the one day a week closing requirement for those businesses
who sell certain goods. Those goods are defined specifically in subss. (
a
)
and (
c
) and defined through the use of common business classifications
in subs. (
b
).

[
78
]

I am convinced that “greenhouses” and “Market
Gardens” are common retail businesses, open on a weekly basis, which indicate
clear demarcations of the type of goods sold on such premises upon reasonable
inquiry and investigation. However, I am not convinced that the classification
“householders garage sale” could ever render an equally clear definition of the
type of goods sold, upon similar inquiry. Rather, it would necessitate the
introduction of personal conjecture and opinion such as to make the definition
impossible. Further, the question remains whether “household garage sales” is a
proper common retail business category at all, in this context, for they are seldomly
open on a weekly basis. Rather, at best, they are open occasionally throughout
the week and usually on the weekend; thus, it would make no sense to apply to
them a one day a week closing requirement.

[
79
]

Finally, I am unable to accept the plaintiffs’
submission that the geographic boundaries used by the by-law to define its
exemptions are also uncertain. Reference to the definition section of the
by-law and to the “area of business establishment” definition provides a method
of investigation which would produce a resolution of whether or not the total
area of the business establishment was of a certain square footage.

[
80
]

This leaves then only the matter of
severability. The principles of severability are concisely stated in
Debaji,

supra, at pp. 148 and 149. That case adopted the statement of principle in
Rogers’ Law of Canadian Municipal Corporations, 2nd ed., vol. 2, at p. 1033.
Succinctly stated it is as follows:

… the parts upheld must form, independently
of the invalid portion, a complete law in some reasonable aspect so that it may
fairly be concluded that the council would have enacted it without the invalid
part.

[
81
]

Looking at the scope of the by-law and the
number of exemptions set out therein after excising the portions of the by-law
which I have ruled to be invalid, I am of the opinion the defendant would have
proceeded with the enactment of such an expurgated edition. Not only the number
of exemptions, but the actual operation of the by-law which permits retailers
to freely choose which day they would be closed, convinces me that the
uncertainty I have found in but two of the exemptions is not fatal. The two
exemptions taken together would not form an integral and indispensable part of
the by-law. Therefore, the invalidity of
s. 2
(
d.
1), s. 6 and the
classification of “householders garage sales” in s. 8(
b
) does not
preclude the case for severance and I am prepared to apply the principles of
severability and not find the total by-law void for uncertainty.

III

[
82
]

Does Red Deer By-law No. 2870/85 violate
s. 2(
a
)
of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
?

[
83
]

This question is answered by reference to the
recent Supreme Court of Canada decision in
R. v. Edwards Books & Art
Ltd.,
(1986)
1986 CanLII 12 (SCC)
, 2 S.C.R. 713, 55 C.R. (3d) 193 (sub nom.
R v. Videoflicks
Ltd.
), 87 C.L.L.C. 14,001, 30 C.C.C. (3d) 385 (sub nom.
Edwards Books
& Art Ltd. v. R; R v. Nortown Foods Ltd.
), 35 D.L.R. (4th) 1, 19 O.A.C.
239, 71 N.R. 161. In applying the principles enunciated in
Edwards Books
to
the case at bar, I conclude that the plaintiffs’ argument that the by-law in
question violates
s. 2(
a
) of the
Charter
must be rejected.

[
84
]

Edwards Books
involved
the constitutionality of Ontario’s Retail Business Holidays Act, R.S.O. 1980,
c. 453. Basically, this Act provided that all retail businesses were required
to close on Sundays unless the business engaged less than seven people in the
service of the public, used less than 5,000 square feet to display and sell
their products and was closed on the preceding Saturday, the “small store exception”.

[
85
]

The Supreme Court examined both the purpose and
effect of the Ontario legislation. The court concluded that the purpose of the
Ontario legislation was secular in nature; the intent was to provide a uniform
holiday, or to use the language of Chief Justice Dickson, “a common pause day”,
for retail employees. Consequently, unlike the Lord’s Day Act in
R. v. Big M
Drug Mart Ltd.
,
(1985)
1985 CanLII 69 (SCC)
, 1 S.C.R. 295, 37 Alta. L.R. (2d) 97, (1985) 3 W.W.R.
481, 18 C.C.C. (3d) 385, 18 D.L.R. (4th) 321, 85 C.L.L.C. 14,023, 13 C.R.R. 64,
60 A.R. 161, 58 N.R. 81, the purpose of the Retail Business Holidays Act was
not found to violate one’s freedom of religion as guaranteed by
s. 2(
a
)
of the
Charter
.

[
86
]

However, what was in issue in
Edwards Books
was
whether the effect of the aforementioned Act was to infringe
s. 2
(
a
).

[
87
]

Mr. Justice Beetz (McIntyre J. concurring) was
of the opinion that the Ontario legislation did not violate
s. 2
(
a
), relying
on the frequently seen reasoning that it is not the legislation that causes a
Saturday observer economic harm, but rather that person’s decision to adhere to
his religious beliefs. Chief Justice Dickson (Chouinard and Le Dain JJ.
concurring) found that the effect of the Ontario legislation was to impose an
indirect economic burden on Saturday observers. Therefore, although the purpose
was secular, the effect was not. As a consequence, the Ontario legislation was
an infringement of
s. 2
(
a
). Both Mr. Justice La Forest and Madame
Justice Wilson agreed with the Chief Justice on this point. Those members of
the court who concluded that
s. 2
(
a
) was violated went on to consider
whether
s. 1
of the
Charter
saved the Ontario legislation. Both the Chief
Justice and La Forest J. were of the opinion that the Ontario legislation was a
reasonable limit within the meaning of s. 1. It was found that the need for a
common pause day was a matter of “pressing and substantial concern”. As well,
in order to achieve its objective, the Act infringed upon freedom of religion
as little as possible. Madame Justice Wilson dissented on this point, holding
that the
s. 2
(
a
) violation was not saved by s. 1.

[
88
]

In considering the issue of the effect of the
legislation, the Chief Justice, writing for the majority, reiterated the
definition of freedom of religion given by the Supreme Court in
Big M Drug
Mart
,
supra, and confirmed that burdens indirectly imposed upon the ability
to practise one’s religion may be prohibited by
s. 2
(
a
). As His Lordship
notes (at p. 34 D.L.R.):

It matters not, I believe, whether a
coercive burden is direct or indirect, intentional or unintentional,
foreseeable or unforeseeable. All coercive burdens on the exercise of religious
beliefs are potentially within the ambit of
s. 2
(
a
).

However, the Chief Justice emphasized that not
all burdens on religious freedom are constitutionally offensive. He went on to
say that “(t)he Constitution shelters individuals and groups only to the extent
that religious beliefs or conduct might reasonably or actually be threatened.”
Therefore, a judicially defined limitation has been placed on
s. 2
(
a
).
The Chief Justice describes the limitation in the following terms (at p. 35
D.L.R.):

… legislative or administrative action
which increases the cost of practising or otherwise manifesting religious
beliefs is not prohibited if the burden is trivial or insubstantial …

Consequently, the test he states for determining
whether the effect of a particular Act or law violates
s. 2
(
a
) is “
…
whether it
significantly impinges on the freedom to manifest or practise religious
beliefs” (at p. 36 D.L.R.).

[
89
]

The Retail Business Holidays Act, in the opinion
of the majority of the Supreme Court, did impose a significant burden on
Saturday observers by making it more expensive for Saturday observers to close
on their sabbath than Sunday observers, given that Saturday observers would
have to close not only on their sabbath but on Sunday as well unless they fell
within the “small store exemption”.

[
90
]

A second form of coercion argued in
Edwards
Books
was that the Ontario legislation “
…
has the direct effect of compelling
non-believers to conform to majoritarian religious dogma, by requiring
retailers to close their stores on Sunday” (at p. 34 D.L.R.). As was held in
Big
M Drug Mart
,
supra,
s. 2
(
a
) includes the “
…
freedom to express and
manifest religious non-belief and the freedom to refuse to participate in
religious practice” (at p. 35 D.L.R.). Chief Justice Dickson refers to this
freedom as “the freedom from conformity to religious dogma” and it essentially
involves the right to abstain from following the tenets of other religions.
However, the Chief Justice warned (at p. 35 D.L.R.) that religious freedom

… is not necessarily impaired by
legislation which requires conduct consistent with the religious beliefs of
another person. One is not being compelled to engage in religious practices
merely because a statutory obligation coincides with the dictates of a
particular religion.

On this basis the Chief Justice rejected the
argument that the Retail Business Holidays Act infringed upon one’s freedom
from conformity to religious dogma because it had a justifiable and
constitutionally valid purpose.

[
91
]

The question in this case is whether the Red
Deer by-law imposes a direct or indirect burden on any individual or group
which would “significantly impinge” upon their “freedom to practise or manifest
religious beliefs.” The by-law basically requires that retail businesses
included within the purview of the by-law close on Sunday unless they close for
at least one day in the following six days. There is no argument from the plaintiffs
regarding the constitutionality of the objectives of the by-law; its purpose
and objective is clearly secular in nature as evidenced by the main recital
clause in the preamble to the by-law, which states:

And
Whereas
the Council of the City of Red Deer wishes to
ensure that at least one day in the week remains substantially free of
commercial activities so that the citizens of Red Deer might benefit thereby
and be permitted to engage in family, social, recreational and other activities
so as to enhance the quality of life and to generally promote the health and
welfare of the citizens in the City of Red Deer …

In addition, the preamble forthrightly expresses
Red Deer city council’s intention that the by-law be secular in nature so as to
conform with the
Charter
. What is in issue, as was in issue in
Edwards
Books,
supra, is whether the
effect
of the by-law is to indirectly
impinge upon one’s freedom of religion.

[
92
]

The plaintiffs argue that by using Sunday as the
day of default, the defendant’s council in effect has “
…
placed the moral power of
the state behind the religions which observe Sunday as a holy day.” The
plaintiffs further argue that if the council’s only objective was to require
businesses to close for one day a week for the purposes stated above, there
would be no need to make reference to Sunday. It would have been easy enough to
require that businesses close one day a week without using Sunday as the start
day or day of default.

[
93
]

The defendant city submits that the choice of
Sunday in s. 4 of the by-law as the starting point is merely a recognition of
the fact that Sunday has historically been the day of rest chosen by the
majority of businesses and industries in Red Deer. Therefore it is reasonable
to presume that Sunday would be the day that most retailers would elect to
close their business. However, the defendant city further argues that the
by-law accommodates all individual or religious preferences by permitting the
individual retailer to choose any day of the week on which to close, therefore

s. 2(
a
) of the
Charter
has not been infringed.

[
94
]

The plaintiffs essentially argue that the by-law
has the effect of taking sides by favouring those who support Sunday as a day
of rest. However, upon a close reading of the by-law’s provisions, one is hard
pressed to find anything to support that argument. Section 4 of the by-law
provides:

On a Sunday, no person shall conduct
business … unless during any period of 24 consecutive hours in the 6 days
immediately following the Sunday the premises are closed to the public …

The by-law basically allows the individual
business to pick any day of the week on which to close its business. Sunday is
merely used as the starting point for the seven-day cycle. Consequently, the
by-law treats all religions equally in that Sunday observers can close on
Sunday and remain open the balance of the week while members of other faiths
who have days of rest other than Sundays can close on that day and remain open
for the rest of the week.

[
95
]

Therefore, a business or individual can meet
both its legal and religious commitments by closing on its day of choice. This
can be accomplished without suffering any additional economic burden in
relation to other religions. It should be recalled that the majority of the
Supreme Court in
Edwards Books
found the Act there in question to
violate
s. 2
(
a
) due to the fact that Saturday observers, in order to
meet their religious and statutory commitments, were forced to close on both
Saturdays and Sundays (unless the small business exemption applied) thereby
incurring an economic penalty not suffered by Sunday observers. In this case,
the by-law has no such indirect effect of placing an economic burden on any
religious group.

[
96
]

The plaintiffs argue that the use of Sunday as a
benchmark is an indirect attempt to influence retailers to close on Sundays in
compliance with majoritarian religious beliefs. The argument basically relies
on Dickson C.J.C.’s freedom from conformity to religious dogma. As mentioned
earlier, the city admits that Sunday was chosen because of the historical
significance of Sunday as the day of rest for the majority of Red Deer
businesses and citizens. However, since a retailer has the option of selecting
any day of the week on which to close his business, it seems unlikely that the
mere reference to Sunday in s. 4 of the by-law could have any influence over a
person’s decision as to which day to close. In addition, even if it is conceded
that the use of Sunday in the by-law has some psychological or compelling
effect on the citizens of Red Deer, it should be recalled that before a
s. 2
(
a
)
infringement is found, there must be a burden placed on the observance or
practice of a particular religion that is not “trivial or insubstantial”. Given
that an individual may select any day of the week to close his business so as
to be in compliance with the by-law, I am of the view that any indirect
psychological attempt at influencing people to conform to majoritarian
Christian views is surely “trivial or insubstantial”. Furthermore, as stated by
Chief Justice Dickson in
Edwards Books
(at p. 36 D.L.R.), “
…
legislation with
a secular inspiration does not abridge the freedom from conformity to religious
dogma merely because statutory provisions coincide with the tenets of a
religion.” Consequently, Red Deer city council’s choice of Sunday as the
benchmark is not an abridgment of one’s freedom from conformity to religious
dogma.

[
97
]

In the result, there is no need to proceed with
a discussion of whether the by-law in question would be saved by
s. 1
of the

Charter
. By applying the principles set forth in
Edwards Books,
supra,
there is only one possible conclusion to reach with respect to the Red Deer
by-law, and that is that it is not an infringement of one’s freedom of
religion. The by-law does not have the effect of favouring one religion to the
detriment of others; all religions are treated equally. The practical effect of
using Sunday in s. 4 of the by-law is the demarcation of the weekly cycle. The
fact that it also happens to coincide with the day on which the majority of Red
Deer citizens observe their sabbath does not render the by-law an infringement
of
s. 2(
a
) of the Charter. The by-law does not “significantly (impinge)
on the freedom to manifest or practise religious beliefs.” In my view, it
promotes one’s freedom of religion by providing an unrestricted choice as to
which day to close. Consequently, the plaintiffs must fail on this ground.

[
98
]

It should be noted that even if it was concluded
that the by-law did infringe s. 2(
a
), the by-law would surely be saved
by s. 1 as being a reasonable limit on one’s freedom of religion. This
conclusion is based on the fact that the Ontario legislation in
Edwards
Books,
supra, although infringing
s. 2
(
a
), was saved by s. 1.
However, the Ontario legislation constituted far more of an infringement on
s.
2
(
a
) than does the by-law in question, given that the Ontario
legislation provided little choice as to which day one could close his business
in order to comply with the Act. Consequently, if the Ontario legislation was a
reasonable limit, then a fortiori, the Red Deer by-law would be a reasonable
limit. However, as concluded above, this case is completely resolved by
reference to
s. 2
(
a
) alone.

IV

[
99
]

I now address the fourth question raised by the
plaintiffs: whether by-law 2870/85 is inconsistent with the equality of rights
provision,
s. 15
, of the
Charter
. The preliminary obstacle the corporate
plaintiffs must overcome in making this argument is that the protections
provided in
s. 15
are not restricted to natural persons or human beings.

Section 15(1)
states that:

15.(1) Every
individual
is equal
before and under the law and has the right to the equal protection and equal
benefit of the law without discrimination and, in particular, without
discrimination based on race, national or ethnic origin, COLOR, religion, sex,
age or mental or physical disability. (emphasis added)

[
100
]

The plaintiffs submit that a broad and generous
interpretation should be afforded the word “individual” which would necessarily
include corporations. Further, they argue that it is relevant that corporations
have received protection under other sections of the
Charter
.

[
101
]

In interpreting the wording of a
Charter
section
great assistance may be gained from this statement by Dickson J. (as he then
was) in
R.
v. Big M Drug Mart
,
supra, (at p. 524 W.W.R.):

In my view this analysis is to be
undertaken, and the purpose of the right or freedom in question is to be
sought, by reference to the character and the larger objects of the
Charter

itself, to the language chosen to articulate the specific right or freedom, to
the historical origins of the concepts enshrined, and where applicable, to the
meaning and purpose of the other specific rights and freedoms with which it is
associated within the text of the Charter. The interpretation should be, as the
judgment in
Southern
emphasizes, a generous rather than a legalistic
one, aimed at fulfilling the purpose of the guarantee and securing for
individuals the full benefit of the Charter’s protection. At the same time it
is important not to overshoot the actual purpose of the right or freedom in
question, but to recall that the Charter was not enacted in a vacuum, and must
therefore, as this court’s decision in
L.S.U.C. v. Skapinker
,
(1984)
1984 CanLII 3 (SCC)
, 1
S.C.R. 357, 11 C.C.C. (3d) 481, 9 D.L.R. (4th) 161, 8 C.R.R. 193, 53 N.R. 169,
3 O.A.C. 321, illustrates, be placed in its proper linguistic, philosophic and
historical contexts.

[
102
]

In considering s. 15(1) in light of other
sections of the
Charter
, particularly
s. 15(2)
and the explicit demarcation of
the heading “Equality Rights” for this section alone, it is most important to
note that the use of the word “individual” is found only in s. 15(1). The
obvious question then to be asked is whether s. 15(1) is to have a different
and possibly more restricted application than the other Charter sections.

[
103
]

In focusing on the language chosen to articulate
the right to equality under s. 15(1) it is clear that the enumerated prohibited
grounds of discrimination in both subsections pertain exclusively to human beings.
Section 15(1) provides protection from discrimination on the grounds of: “race,
national or ethnic origin, COLOR, religion, sex, age or mental or physical
disability.” It is recognized that this list is not exhaustive, as it is
preceded by the words “in particular”; however, given that the entire and
fairly lengthy list relates to human characteristics, a strong argument can be
made that the ejusdem generis rule applies.

[
104
]

Additional support for restricting the meaning
of “individual” to natural persons is found in the historical background which
led to the implementation of s. 15(1). Evidence of the legislative history of
the Constitution was admitted by the Supreme Court of Canada in
Dubois v.
R.,
(1985)
1985 CanLII 10 (SCC)
, 2 S.C.R. 350, 41 Alta. L.R. (2d) 97, (1986) 1 W.W.R. 193, 48
C.R. (3d) 193, 22 C.C.C. (3d) 513, 23 D.L.R. (4th) 503, 18 C.R.R. 1, 66 A.R.
202, 62 N.R. 50, as the court looked at a previous draft of
s. 13
of the

Charter
as an aid to interpretation. Further, in
Re B.C. Motor Vehicle Act,
(1985)

1985 CanLII 81 (SCC)
, 2 S.C.R. 486, (1986) 1 W.W.R. 481 (sub nom.
Ref. re S. 94(2) of Motor
Vehicle Act
), 69 B.C.L.R. 145, 48 C.R. (3d) 289, 36 M.V.R. 240, 23 C.C.C.
(3d) 289, 24 D.L.R. (4th) 536, 18 C.R.R. 30, 63 N.R. 266, the Supreme Court of
Canada admitted into evidence statements of the Minister of Justice and senior
officials within the Department of Justice before the Special Joint Committee
of the Senate and the House of Commons on the Constitution of Canada and with
respect to their interpretation of s. 7 of the then proposed Charter. The
question then became one of the weight to be awarded such evidence and because
of the concern over determining the common intention of a legislative body
which involves an “enormous multiplicity of actors”, the evidence was given
“minimal weight” (at 508-509 S.C.R.).

[
105
]

In reviewing statements of the Minister of
Justice and senior officials within the Department of Justice before the
Special Joint Committee on the Constitution with respect to their
interpretation of s. 15(1) of the then proposed
Charter
it is significant that
all political parties were in agreement that
s. 15(1)
should have the
restricted application to natural persons. The only debate concerned which word
would best express their intentions. As stated by Mr. Robinson in the 32nd Parliament,
1st Session, 1980-81 Proceedings, Issue Nos. 26-45 on 23rd January 1981, at
44:7:

Section 15 originally read “everyone” and
the government, and I certainly think the government correctly changed those
words to “every individual” and the explanatory notes read:

“The word ‘everyone’ would be replaced by
the word ‘every individual’ to make it clear that this right would apply to
natural persons only.”

[
106
]

Therefore, in light of the common intentions of
all debating the interpretation of s. 15(1) this evidence can be given more
than “minimal weight” in aiding in the interpretation of “individual”.

[
107
]

The plaintiffs submit that the use of the word “personne”
in the French version of s. 15(1) permits the inclusion of corporations. They
argue that support for this interpretation can be found in the federal
Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-23, which specifically includes
corporations in the definition of “personne”, and that the word “personne” in
the context of
s. 24(1)
of the
Charter
has been interpreted to include
corporations:
R. v. G.B.,
1983 CanLII 1013 (AB QB)
, 24 Alta. L.R. (2d) 226, (1983) 3 W.W.R. 141, 4
C.C.C. (3d) 59 (sub nom.
Re Edmonton Journal and AG. Alta.),
146 D.L.R.
(3d) 673 at 675, 14 C.R.R. 296 at 298, 42 A.R. 383 (Q.B.). An argument may then
be made that the Supreme Court of Canada’s decision in
R. v. Collins,
(1987)

1987 CanLII 84 (SCC)
, 1 S.C.R. 265, (1987) 3 W.W.R. 699, 13 B.C.L.R. (2d) 1, 56 C.R. (3d) 193, 33
C.C.C. (3d) 1, 74 N.R. 276, should be followed, in which it was held that
reference should be made to both the English and French text and the court
should favour the interpretation which best protects the right; the least
onerous test.

[
108
]

Although the Interpretation Act may suggest a
line of interpretation, neither the federal nor provincial Acts apply to the
Constitution:
L.S.U.C. v. Skapinker

(supra), at p. 370 S.C.R. Further
and more importantly, this argument totally disregards the context in which “personne”
is used. Again, because of the prohibition of discrimination on the grounds of
human characteristics, the more logical interpretation of “personne” would be
that of a natural person.

[
109
]

Finally, the majority of decisions addressing
the issue have excluded corporations from the definition of “individual” in
s.
15
:
Aerlinte Eireanne Teoranta v. Can.
(1987),
1987 CanLII 8912 (FC)
, 9 F.T.R. 29 (Fed. T.D.);
Smith,
Kline & French Laboratories Ltd. v. Can. (A.G.),
(1986)

, 1 F.C. 274, 7
C.P.R. (3d) 145, 24 D.L.R. (4th) 321, 19 C.R.R. 233 (T.D.);
Nissho Corp. v.
Bank of B.C.,
Alta. Q.B., No. 8603-12287, 14th May 1987 (not yet reported);

Mund v. Medicine Hat
(1985),
1985 CanLII 1413 (AB QB)
, 67 A.R. 11 (Q.B.);
Milk Bd. v. Clearview
Dairy Farm Inc.,
(1987)

, 4 W.W.R. 279, 12 B.C.L.R. (2d) 116 (C.A.);
Homemade
Winecrafts (Can.) Ltd. v. B.C. (A.G.)
(1986),
1986 CanLII 1284 (BC SC)
, 26 D.L.R. (4th) 468
(B.C.S.C.);
Surrey Credit Union v. Mendonca
(1985),
1985 CanLII 264 (BC SC)
, 67 B.C.L.R. 310, 19
C.R.R. 230 (S.C.);
Gerald Shapiro Hldgs. Inc. v. Nathan Tessis & Assoc.
Inc.,
No. 21985/84, 18th November 1986 (now reported
13 C.P.C. (2d) 288, 27
C.R.R. 161
) (Ont. Master);
K Mart Can. Ltd. v. Millmink Devs. Ltd.,
1986 CanLII 2841 (ON HCJ)
, 56
O.R. (2d) 422, 24 C.C.L.I. 139,
(1986) I.L.R. 1-2114, 11 C.P.C. (2d) 243, 31
D.L.R. (4th) 135 (H.C.)
;
Aluminum Co. of Can. v. Ont. (Min. of Environment)
(1986),

1986 CanLII 2833 (ON HCJ)
, 55 O.R. (2d) 522, 19 Admin. L.R. 192, 1 C.E.L.R. (N.S.) 1, 29 D.L.R. (4th) 583,
25 C.R.R. 50, 16 O.A.C. 14 (Div. Ct.);
l’Assn Des Detaillants en
Alimentation du Que. v. La Ferme Camaval Inc.,
No. 500-05-009768-852, 6th
August 1986 (now reported
(1986) R.J.Q. 2513
) (S.C.);
Kurolak v. Sask. (Min.
of Highways & Tpt.),
(1986)
1986 CanLII 3558 (SK QB)
, 4 W.W.R. 323, 28 D.L.R. (4th) 273, 48 Sask.
R. 92 (Q.B.).

[
110
]

Only the trial judge in
Milk Bd. v. Clearview
Dairy Farms Inc.
(1986), 69 B.C.L.R. 220 (S.C.), at pp. 245-46
expressly
included corporations within the protection of
s. 15
and this finding was
overturned by the British Columbia Court of Appeal, supra.

[
111
]

Therefore, keeping in mind the “linguistic”
contexts of s. 15(1) it is clear that only natural persons are to be protected
under the
Charter
’s equality provisions. Insufficient evidence as to the
historic or philosophic contexts was submitted to permit a proposed inquiry
into those matters. Hence, I find the corporate plaintiffs do not have a right
protected under
s. 15
which could potentially be infringed.

[
112
]

Accordingly, the plaintiffs are restrained from
seeking relief under s. 24(1), as it only provides a remedy to a party who has
been granted rights under the
Charter
and whose rights, in turn, have been
offended.

[
113
]

The plaintiffs further submit that the generally
applied standing principles would allow a corporation to raise s. 15 regardless
of whether “individual” includes corporations. They assert that by virtue of
s.
52
, the
Charter
governs all laws applied by the courts regardless of the nature
of the parties before them. They argue that authority for this proposition may
be derived from Dickson J. (as he then was) in
Big M Drug Mart
,
supra,
at p. 499 (W.W.R.) when he stated that “(it) is the nature of the law, not the
status of the
accused,
that is in issue” (emphasis added).

[
114
]

In examining Dickson J.’s statement it is most
evidently restricted to a situation involving a party facing criminal
prosecution, which is not the situation in this case. As he stated earlier in
his judgment (at p. 498 W.W.R.):

Section 52 sets out the fundamental
principle of constitutional law that the Constitution is supreme. The undoubted
corollary to be drawn from this principle is that no one can be convicted of an
offence under an unconstitutional law.
The respondent did not come to court
voluntarily as an interested citizen asking for a prerogative declaration that
a statute is unconstitutional.
If it had been engaged in such “public
interest litigation” it would have had to fulfil the status requirements laid
down by this court in the trilogy of “standing” cases (
Thorson v. A.G. Can.,

(1975)
1974 CanLII 6 (SCC)
, 1 S.C.R. 138, 43 D.L.R. (3d) 1, 1 N.R. 225;
N.S. Bd. of Censors
v. McNeil,
(1976)
1975 CanLII 14 (SCC)
, 2 S.C.R. 265, 32 C.R.N.S. 376, 55 D.L.R. (3d) 632, 12
N.S.R. (2d) 85, 5 N.R. 43; and
Min. of Justice of Can. v. Borowski,
(1981)

1981 CanLII 34 (SCC)
, 2 S.C.R. 575, (1982) 1 W.W.R. 97, 24 C.R. (3d) 352, 24 C.P.C. 62, 64 C.C.C.
(2d) 97, 130 D.L.R. (3d) 588, 12 Sask. R. 420, 39 N.R. 331) but that was not
the reason for its appearance in court. (emphasis added)

[
115
]

Therefore, because the case at bar involves
plaintiffs seeking a prerogative declaration that by-law 2870/85 is
unconstitutional, they will have to satisfy the status requirements laid down
by the courts in the cases of
Thorson
, McNeil
and
Borowski.

[
116
]

In
Borowski
,
supra (at p. 598 S.C.R.), Martland
J. enunciates the requirements for standing which are drawn from the three
cases:

I interpret (
Thorson
and
McNeil
)
as deciding that to establish status as a plaintiff in a suit seeking a
declaration that legislation is invalid, if there is a serious issue as to its
invalidity, a person need only to show that he is affected by it directly or
that
he has a genuine interest as a citizen in the validity of the legislation and
that there is no other reasonable and effective manner in which the issue may
be brought before the Court.
(emphasis added)

[
117
]

The plaintiffs are obviously not parties
directly affected, as on my determination they have no s. 15(1) rights to be
infringed. Ultimately, they could be directly affected if they chose to breach
the by-law and they were then charged but that is only speculation at this
time. As well the plaintiffs may be successful in arguing that this is public
interest litigation, and that they have a genuine interest as a citizen in the
validity of the legislation, but I do not think that this is the most
reasonable and effective manner in which this issue may be brought before the
court. Clearly there will be natural persons caught by the restrictions of
by-law 2870/85 (sole proprietors with stores larger than 3,000 square feet)
whose
s. 15(1)

Charter
rights may arguably be infringed. They are the
“individuals” who would provide the most reasonable avenue for this matter to
be brought before the court and therefore it would be inappropriate to exercise
judicial discretion in favour of the plaintiffs’ assertion of standing. It is
noted that the Alberta Queen’s Bench in
Cabre Exploration Ltd. v. Arndt,
1986 CanLII 1642 (AB QB)
, 44
Alta. L.R. (2d) 250, (1986) 4 W.W.R. 261 at 265, 28 D.L.R. (4th) 747, 35 L.C.R.
213, 22 C.R.R. 319, 69 A.R. 296, granted a corporation standing to argue that

s. 15
was violated by s. 26(9) of the Surface Rights Act. Dea J. stated:

In the case at bar, the applicant operator
is not involved in “public interest litigation”. As well, the applicant
operator is not an accused person nor can it be said that it is the only party
with rights that are potentially violated under
s. 15
, as all operators find
themselves in that condition. It claims standing on the basis (inter alia) that
it has a direct pecuniary interest in the constitutional validity of s. 26(9)
of the Surface Rights Act.

The circumstances of the applicant operator
are as follows. Because of the intervention of the Surface Rights Act, the
operator cannot exercise its common law right of entry to work its minerals
unless it first secures the consent of the owner or obtains a right of entry
order under the Surface Rights Act. Here, a right of entry order was obtained
and, following that, the Surface Rights Board determined the compensation
payable by the operator to the owner. The operator appealed that determination
to this court and the compensation has in fact been varied.
In accordance
with s. 26(9), the costs of the appeal are (subject to special circumstances)
payable on a solicitor-client basis to the owner by the operator “
…

regardless of the result”.
Obviously, the operator has a direct pecuniary
interest in the validity or the invalidity of the impugned section in the
Surface Rights Act. (emphasis added)

[
118
]

So in this case, it appears Dea J. accorded
status to Cabre Exploration Ltd. to put in issue the equality provisions of
s.
15
of the
Charter
because under the provisions of the legislation it was being
“penalized” costs regardless of the results of the litigation necessary to
exercise its development rights. The situation is akin to that of being
prosecuted so that there could be no issue as to its standing to raise a defence
to the penalty imposed by the form of the legislation under attack.

[
119
]

Such is not the case in this proceeding which
seeks only declaratory relief and no protection from prosecution or imposition
of penalty.

[
120
]

In summary, the corporate plaintiffs have failed
to show that they are “individuals” so as to be protected by
s. 15(1)
of the

Charter
. Therefore, they will not be permitted to resort to s. 24(1) for
relief. Further, they have not satisfied the status requirements established by
the Supreme Court of Canada in the cases of
Thorson
, McNeil,
and
Borowski,

and thus will be precluded from relying on s. 52 to have by-law 2870/85
rendered of no force and effect.

Conclusion

[
121
]

In the result, I declare by-law 2870/85 of the
city of Red Deer valid except for those portions I have found to be uncertain
and which I have severed.
